text: How to read this chapter
This chapter is orientation, not science. It explains how the Handbook grades evidence and where its limits are. The science starts in Exercise science.
The problem this Handbook solves

Fitness does not lack information. The information is unsorted. A careful review of many trials and a confident video reach you through the same feed, in the same format, with the same air of authority. Nothing tells you which claim rests on twenty trials and which rests on an explanation someone found plausible.

The result is rarely that people fail to train. They train for years while changing what they do, and never build enough uninterrupted progress in one direction to see a result. What is usually missing is not effort. It is a stable framework, and a way to tell strong claims from weak ones.
This Handbook aims to tell you what to do, and also how confident anyone should be that it works.
What this Handbook is
It is a reference covering training, nutrition, recovery, physique and tracking progress. Your Levlofit plan tells you what to do today. The Handbook explains why.
Property | What it means for you
Property: It explains; What it means for you: Recommendations come with their reasoning, so you can adapt them when your situation differs.
Property: It grades its confidence; What it means for you: Where the evidence is weak or divided, it says so instead of choosing a side to read better.
Property: It is made to be re-read; What it means for you: What is useful to you changes as you train for longer.
How evidence is graded
Claims carry one of six grades. These are the Handbook's own reading of the sources, not grades given by the papers.
Grade | What it means | Wording used
Grade: Strong; What it means: Several good reviews, or a current position stand from a recognised body.; Wording used: "Evidence shows"
Grade: Moderate; What it means: Consistent findings with real limits.; Wording used: "Evidence suggests"
Grade: Emerging; What it means: Early human evidence.; Wording used: "Early evidence indicates"
Grade: Insufficient; What it means: No adequate human evidence either way.; Wording used: "Not established"
Grade: Contested; What it means: Credible evidence on both sides.; Wording used: "Evidence is divided"
Grade: Practical; What it means: Sensible guidance, or personal preference, that research has not settled.; Wording used: "In practice"

Two rules follow. An explanation of how something might work inside the body is not a result, and does not justify a recommendation by itself. And "not established" means the question is open, not that the answer is no.
A useful habit
When you meet a confident fitness claim, do not ask only whether it is true. Ask what someone would have had to measure to know it. Many popular claims fail that question straight away.
Five working principles
These are working defaults, not scientific findings.
Consistency beats intensity. The plan you follow for two years beats the better plan you follow for six weeks.
Technique defines the load. A repetition done differently is a different exercise, whatever the log says.
Recovery is part of training. It is an input to adaptation, not a reward for having trained.
Progress is measured in months. Change from week to week is mostly noise: water, sleep, food timing and measuring error.
Evidence first, then what you will keep doing. Where the evidence is absent, choose the option you will actually sustain.
What progress looks like

One number makes a poor target. Body weight cannot separate muscle gained from food eaten, and a mirror cannot separate real change from better lighting. Track several things, because they move at different speeds and rarely all stall at once.
What to track | What good looks like | Rough timescale
What to track: Strength; What good looks like: More work at the same standard of technique, on the same exercises.; Rough timescale: Weeks
What to track: Physique; What good looks like: Balanced development, with body fat controlled rather than as low as possible.; Rough timescale: Months
What to track: Health; What good looks like: Fitness, joint comfort and everyday movement improving or holding.; Rough timescale: Months
What to track: Recovery; What good looks like: Handling more training than a year ago without building up fatigue.; Rough timescale: Months to years
What to track: Sustainability; What good looks like: Still training, still enjoying it, still free of injury, years later.; Rough timescale: Years
The last row decides the others.
How to use this Handbook
Read this volume in order. The next few chapters give you the words every later chapter uses.
Use the rest as reference. Go to the chapter that answers the question you have now.
Check the grade before acting. A moderate claim deserves a trial in your training. An insufficient one deserves curiosity, not a change of plan.
Change one thing at a time. Two changes together give a result you cannot explain.
Re-read the basics. They become more useful as you train for longer.
Scope and limits
What this Handbook is not
This is general information for healthy adults. It does not diagnose conditions, read medical or lab results, or give individual medical, psychological or clinical nutrition advice.

See a qualified health professional before starting or continuing if you have a diagnosed condition, are pregnant or have recently given birth, are managing an injury, have pain during exercise, or have a history of disordered eating. Nothing here should delay care you would otherwise seek.

Much of the research behind this Handbook studied young adults, more often men, over weeks to months. The further you are from that description, the more carefully you should apply it. Food examples are written for Indian kitchens and budgets. That shapes the examples, not the science.
Key takeaways
The problem is unsorted information, not missing information.
Claims carry a visible grade. Check it before acting.
An explanation is not a result, and "not established" does not mean false.
Progress has several parts and is measured in months. Sustainability decides the rest.
This is education, not clinical care.

text: Your heart-rate zones
A simple estimate of your maximum heart rate is 208 minus 0.7 times your age. It is an estimate: your real maximum can be 10 beats or more either way.
Intensity by % of maximum heart rate
50 · 57 · Very light: easy walking [% of max]
57 · 64 · Light: warm-ups, brisk walking [% of max]
64 · 77 · Moderate: you can talk in sentences [% of max]
77 · 96 · Vigorous: a few words at a time [% of max]

208 - 0.7 x age · bpm · estimated maximum heart rate

text: How far to trust calories burned
Error in energy burned, 7 wrist devices tested
Most accurate device · 27 · still off by about a quarter [% average error]
Least accurate device · 93 · nearly double or near zero [% average error]

In a test of seven popular wrist devices, heart rate was fairly accurate but none measured energy burned well; even the best was off by about a quarter. Gym machines and class estimates use averages that ignore your size and fitness, so they are no better. Treat calories-burned numbers as rough, and never "eat back" all of them. Judge your intake by the trend in your body weight instead.

Mixing the two well
Cardio does not kill gains · Adding cardio to lifting does not reduce muscle growth overall; very large amounts of running may slightly reduce leg strength gains.
Do the priority first · Whatever you most want to improve goes first in the session, while you are fresh.
Separate hard sessions · Hard intervals and heavy leg days are best on different days, or 6 hours or more apart.

text: A warm-up has one well-supported benefit: a better session. Other benefits are claimed on much weaker grounds. This chapter separates them and gives you a warm-up short enough that you will keep doing it.
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Mobility is here because the two get confused. A warm-up prepares you for today. Mobility work changes your range over months.

chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Injury risk
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: "Warm up so you do not get injured" is the most repeated reason, and not a secure one. Do not count on a warm-up or stretching to protect you.
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: The stronger evidence points to strength training itself. Across six randomised trials with 7,738 people aged 12 to 40, it cut sports injury risk by about two thirds (relative risk 0.338, 0.238 to 0.480), and more training was linked with more protection. Most of those people were athletes, so applying this to gym training is a reasonable step, not a tested one.
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021
supporting_passage: Results Six studies analysed five different interventions with four distinct outcomes. 7738 participants aged 12-40 years were included and sustained 177 acute or overuse injuries. [...] Cluster-adjusted intention-to-treat analysis established RR 0.338 (0.238-0.480).

text: Dynamic and static stretching
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Dynamic stretching moves a joint through its range under control, such as leg swings, arm circles, bodyweight squats and walking lunges. Static stretching holds a stretched position still.

text: Approach | Effect on jumping and sprinting
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Approach: Static, then dynamic; Effect on jumping and sprinting: Ranked highest for jump height, and clearly better than no warm-up.

chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: In practice:
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: If a stretch lets you reach a position you otherwise cannot, use it, keep it short, then do dynamic movement and warm-up sets.
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: If you have no such limit, dynamic work alone is enough and faster.
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Avoid long static holds as your only preparation right before heavy or explosive work.
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: These studies measured jumping and sprinting, which may react more than an ordinary set of 8 to 12 repetitions.

text: A warm-up in four stages
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Stage | Time | Purpose
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Stage: General; Time: 3 to 5 min; Purpose: Light continuous activity to raise temperature.
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Stage: Dynamic mobility; Time: 4 to 6 min; Purpose: Controlled movement through the ranges you will use today.
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Stage: Activation; Time: 0 to 5 min; Purpose: Optional light work for muscles you struggle to feel.
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Stage: Warm-up sets; Time: 5 to 10 min; Purpose: Your first big lift, with gradually heavier loads.
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: These times are practical guides. Warm-up sets matter most, and they are the stage people skip. They rehearse the exact movement, and they tell you something: when a normal load feels heavy today, you find out before committing to a hard set. If you are short of time, cut the general stage, not these.
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: On activation drills
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Glute bridges before squats and band work before pressing are popular and cheap. It is not established that they add anything beyond warm-up sets. Keep them if they help you. Drop them before you drop your warm-up sets.
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Later exercises in a session need only one or two light sets.
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Mobility
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Mobility is the range you can actively reach and control. Range you can only be pushed into is not much use under load.
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Evidence: moderate
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: A review of 65 studies found stretching does not lengthen muscle: fascicle length did not change after one session or many. Stiffness fell after both. Tolerance to the stretch rose only after repeated stretching.

[...] Static stretching alone does not appear to increase fascicle length.. .

text: What this means for you:
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Train mobility separately. A warm-up uses the range you have. New range takes weeks to months.
chapter_sources: rodrigues2022 li2023 ingram2025 lauersen2018 behm2016 konrad2024 afonso2021

text: Pick a method you will keep up. Regular practice matters. Exact hold times matter less than people claim.

text: Rep ranges
What different rep ranges are best at
1 to 5 · Maximal strength · Heaviest loads; most skill practice for heavy lifts; long rests.
6 to 12 · Muscle and strength together · The most time-efficient range for most people.
12 to 20 · Muscle, endurance · Builds as much muscle as heavier sets when taken close to failure; burns more.
20 to 30 or more · Muscle, endurance · Works too, but sets are long and uncomfortable.

Light and heavy sets build similar muscle when each set ends close to failure; heavy sets build more maximal strength. No rep range "tones" or "burns fat": fat loss comes from eating less. Most good programmes mix ranges.
Should you train to failure?
How close to failure to stop
0 · 1 · Failure: fine on safe isolation moves now and then [reps left in reserve]
1 · 3 · Where most sets should end: close enough to grow [reps left in reserve]
3 · 5 · Good for heavy compound lifts while learning technique [reps left in reserve]
5 · 8 · Too easy to drive much growth [reps left in reserve]

Sets stopped 1 to 3 reps short of failure build about as much muscle as sets to failure, with less fatigue. People misjudge how close they are, so take a set to failure now and then on a safe move to calibrate. Beginners should not grind squats, deadlifts or presses to failure while learning them.

text: Chapter overview
Rest is one input to recovery. Recovery is the outcome: fatigue clears, and the signal from training turns into adaptation.
This chapter covers what has real evidence, says where the evidence is thinner than the fitness industry suggests, and gives you signals you can actually watch.
What recovery is

A hard session creates a signal to adapt, and it creates fatigue. What you feel in the next day or two is mostly the fatigue. Recovery depends on sleep, on eating enough, and on not stacking another big demand too soon.
Without a real training signal, sleep and protein have nothing to act on. Recovery decides how much of the signal is carried out.
Sleep
Sleep has clear evidence behind it for training performance, and it is often the first thing people trade away.
Evidence: moderate

A review of 69 publications found sleep loss lowered exercise performance by about 7.6% on average, across every category tested. Performance fell about 0.4% for each extra hour awake before exercise. The effects were consistent for going without sleep or waking earlier than normal, and less consistent for going to bed late. Results varied widely between studies and 89% of participants were men, so the size for any one person is uncertain.
supporting_passage: Specifically, we found that on average, exercise performance declined by ~ 0.4% per hour following sleep loss (note, this result is not inflated by the skill category because 8/13 of these tasks were performed following an early-restriction protocol). [...] A significant positive relationship was observed between time awake prior to the exercise task and % Δ in performance for both deprivation and late-restriction protocols (~ 0.4% decrease for every hour awake prior to exercise).

text: One finding helps with planning: afternoon and evening sessions after a poor night consistently suffered, while morning sessions were largely unaffected. If a bad night is unavoidable, train earlier if you can.

text: Evidence: insufficient on sleep and injury

You will often hear that poor sleep raises injury risk. A review of 12 cohort studies concluded that current evidence does not support poor sleep as an independent risk factor for injury in adult athletes, while noting the studies were too mixed to settle the question.
supporting_passage: Results From our review of 12 prospective cohort studies, we found limited evidence supporting an association between poor sleep and injury in adult athletic populations. [...] Conclusions The current evidence does not support poor sleep as an independent risk factor for increased risk of sport or physical training-related injuries in adult athletic populations.

text: This is no argument for sleeping less. The case for sleep rests on performance, which has good support.
Practical habits
These are practical habits, not findings from the papers above.
Keep your wake time steady, including at weekends.
Give yourself enough time in bed. You control that directly.
Keep your room dark and cool.
If late caffeine or alcohol affects your sleep, move or drop it.
Food

Recovery has a material cost. Energy decides whether your body has resources to build. Gaining muscle while eating well below your needs is possible in some situations and harder in others. Protein supplies what repair and building use. Protein gives the amounts and Indian sources.
How you organise training
The biggest recovery lever you control is how much you asked for in training.
Lever | Effect on recovery demand
Lever: Weekly hard sets; Effect on recovery demand: The main driver. More volume brings more signal and more cost.
Lever: Closeness to failure; Effect on recovery demand: Failure adds fatigue, and has not been shown to give consistently better results.
supporting_passage: Training to momentary muscle fatigue, equipment type, exercise complexity, set structure, time under tension, blood flow restriction, and periodization did not consistently impact training outcomes.
reviewed_by: Claude (session 2026-11-07, AI, not a qualified reviewer); passage matched in the downloaded source text
notes: The quoted passage supports part of this claim; the rest of it is not covered by this quote.

text: Lever: Exercise choice; Effect on recovery demand: In practice, heavy compound lifts tire you more per set than machine isolation work.
Lever: Spreading sets out; Effect on recovery demand: The same weekly sets over more days can keep later sets from fading.

Rest days are part of the plan. They need not be still: walking and ordinary activity are fine. They do need to be easier than a training day. A "light" day that becomes a hard session is an unlogged training day.
Life stress

Exams, work and personal pressure can reduce how much training you can handle, even if your plan has not changed. In practice, let volume move with your life. Cutting sets during a hard month and restoring them later keeps you consistent. Holding volume and missing sessions does not.
Reading your own signals

No home device directly measures recovery. Treat sleep scores and readiness numbers as weak inputs, and do not let them overrule your logged performance. These practical signals are cheaper and more useful:
Signal | Recovering well | Under-recovered
Signal: Session performance; Recovering well: Load or repetitions rising over weeks, with an occasional flat day; Under-recovered: Several unrelated exercises falling for over a week
Signal: Warm-up; Recovering well: Warm-up sets feel normal; Under-recovered: Normal warm-up loads feel heavy
Signal: Joints; Recovering well: Quiet, or briefly stiff then fine; Under-recovered: Aches that outlast sessions and build week to week
Signal: Sleep; Recovering well: Falling asleep normally, waking fairly rested; Under-recovered: Trouble falling asleep, or waking early despite being tired
Signal: Appetite and mood; Recovering well: Steady; Under-recovered: Both low for several days with no other reason
One bad session is noise. A week of them across several exercises, plus two or more other rows, is worth acting on. See Deload week.
What recovery is not
Soreness is not a recovery reading. It often reflects unfamiliar work.

Recovery tools are not recovery. Do not expect massage guns or similar tools to replace sleep and food. Regular cold-water immersion had a harmful effect on strength gains from resistance training in one review (effect size -0.60, -0.87 to -0.33), so avoid making it a habit if strength is your goal.

text: Total inactivity is not required. Light movement is fine.
Supplements do not replace the basics. They do not make up for too little sleep or food.
When to get help
Beyond a training adjustment
Ordinary fatigue responds to less training. These do not. See a qualified clinician:
Sharp, localised or lasting pain, especially at rest or at night.
Numbness, tingling or weakness in a specific pattern.
Fatigue, unexplained weight loss or falling performance that continues after several weeks of truly reduced training.
Missed periods, frequent illness or bone pain alongside low food intake. These may point to low energy availability, which is a medical concern.
Distress about food, weight or missed sessions that affects daily life.
This Handbook does not diagnose and does not replace individual care.
Key takeaways
Recovery turns a training signal into adaptation.
Sleep loss lowers performance, more so for afternoon and evening sessions.
It is not established that poor sleep alone raises injury risk.
Your biggest recovery lever is how much you asked for in training.
Soreness and readiness scores are weak signals. Logged performance across exercises is stronger.
Lasting pain, nerve symptoms or fatigue that survives real rest are medical questions.

text: What a pull session trains
A pull session trains the muscles that draw weight toward you: lats, middle and upper back, rear shoulders, biceps and forearms.

Back training is often sold as a fix for desk posture. It is not established that strengthening your back changes your usual posture, or that doing so would bring a health or performance benefit. Train your back because it is a large part of your muscle, because balanced development is a fair goal, and because pulling strength is worth having.
Slots
A pull session uses slots too, for the same reasons as Building a push session: order helps strength, and different exercises may develop different parts of a muscle.

Include both vertical pulling (pulldowns, pull-ups) and horizontal pulling (rows), because they load your back along different lines. "Pulldowns for width, rows for thickness" is gym shorthand that no study measured. Do both for coverage.
Slot | Job
Slot: Main pull; Job: The heaviest, most technical pull, done first.
Slot: Second pull; Job: The pattern the main pull did not use.
Slot: Lat work; Job: A machine or cable movement through a full range.
Slot: Rear shoulder; Job: Direct work, because pulling gives it limited work.
Slot: Biceps; Job: Direct arm work, once your back is no longer the limit.
Choosing an exercise
The same four tests apply: equipment, joints, skill and fatigue. Three points are specific to pulling:
A pull-up or barbell row asks more skill and grip than a machine row or pulldown. With less experience or energy, the supported option is a fair choice.
Grip can end the set first. If your hands give out before your back, your back has not done the work you intended. Straps, a different grip or a machine all solve this.
The main slot is where a hard, technical movement is cheapest, because you are freshest.
Swapping exercises

A wide-grip pulldown and a pull-up can replace each other. Both are vertical pulls with the same joint actions, though the pull-up asks more stability. A seated cable row cannot replace either. It is a horizontal pull, so it belongs in the second slot.
Volume, effort and frequency
The evidence in Building a push session applies unchanged.

One point matters more here: biceps get work from every pulling set. Counted as half a set each, heavy rows and pulldowns already give your biceps real volume before your first curl. Counting indirect sets this way predicted results best in one large review.

How to progress

The three models from the push chapter apply. Pulling adds one wrinkle: bodyweight moves go up in big steps. You cannot add a small amount to a pull-up as you can on a pulldown, so add repetitions first and only add weight when your range is full. Assisted versions allow finer steps.
Warm-up
Use the same three parts, aimed at your shoulders, upper back and grip. Warm-up sets matter most.
Across the week

A pull session shares recovery with anything that loads your biceps, forearms or the back of your body, including heavy Romanian deadlifts on leg day. Plan by the muscles you actually trained, using the signals in Recovery, not a fixed number of hours.
Worked example
This is one example, not a prescription.
Slot | Exercise | Sets | Repetitions | Rest
Slot: Main pull (vertical); Exercise: Pull-up or assisted pull-up; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 6 to 10; Rest: 2 to 3 min
Slot: Second pull (horizontal); Exercise: Chest-supported row; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 8 to 10; Rest: 2 min
Slot: Lat work; Exercise: Neutral-grip lat pulldown; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 10 to 12; Rest: 90 sec
Slot: Rear shoulder; Exercise: Face pull; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 12 to 15; Rest: 60 to 90 sec
Slot: Biceps; Exercise: Incline dumbbell curl; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 10 to 12; Rest: 75 to 90 sec
Slot: Biceps; Exercise: Hammer curl; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 10 to 12; Rest: 75 to 90 sec

Your upper arm stays behind your body on an incline curl, which loads the biceps at a longer length. Partial repetitions at long muscle lengths gave more growth than those at short lengths in one review, though that does not directly test this exercise.
Six direct biceps sets look modest until you count the nine pulling sets at half each. That makes about 10.5 biceps sets from this session.
Common mistakes
Swinging. It moves the load onto your lower back and hips.
Pulling with your arms. Start the movement from your shoulder blades.
Using more load than your grip can hold. The set ends before your back has worked.
Skipping rear shoulder work. It needs its own slot.
Adding curls to fix stalled arms. Check your total pulling sets first.
Using one pattern for both pull slots. Two rows or two pulldowns cover only one line of pull.
Key takeaways
Cover both vertical and horizontal pulling.
Back training does not need a posture claim to justify it.
Every pulling set also trains your biceps. Count it as half.
Grip limits are real. Solve them instead of pushing through.
Recovery follows the muscles you trained, not the name of the session.
What a leg session trains
A leg session trains your quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes and calves. These include some of your largest muscles, and their big lifts are among the hardest most people do, so order matters a lot.
Slots and coverage

Go from the heaviest, most technical lift down to single-joint work that handles fatigue well. Include a squat pattern and a hip hinge, because they load the front and back of your leg in different ways.
Evidence: emerging

Thirty trained people did different exercises with each leg, twice a week for 8 weeks. Leg extension favoured the rectus femoris, part of the quadriceps. Leg press favoured the vastus lateralis, another part. Straight-leg calf raises favoured one calf muscle, the medial gastrocnemius, with no clear result for the lateral gastrocnemius or soleus. This is a single study.
So big lifts may not make isolation work unnecessary, and the reverse may be true too.
Slot | Job
Slot: Main squat pattern; Job: The heaviest, most technical lift, done first.
Slot: Hip hinge; Job: Hamstrings and glutes, which the squat pattern does not fully cover.
Slot: Second quad lift; Job: Usually a machine, adding quad work at lower technical cost.
Slot: Hamstring isolation; Job: Direct knee-bending work.
Slot: Quad isolation; Job: Direct knee-straightening work.
Slot: Calves; Job: A straight-leg raise, a bent-knee raise, or both if you have the equipment.
Filling two slots with squat patterns and skipping the hinge trains the front of your leg twice and neglects the back.
Choosing an exercise

The four tests from Building a push session apply. Joints matter especially here: a barbell squat loads your spine in a way a leg press or hack squat does not, so a lower-back problem can be reason enough to choose the supported option.
Swapping exercises

A barbell back squat and a hack squat can replace each other. Both are squat patterns using your knees and hips. A leg press cannot replace a Romanian deadlift: one is a squat pattern and the other a hinge. Swapping them leaves the hinge slot empty.
Range of motion and partial repetitions
Full range is the default. The ACSM found strength improved with a complete range of motion, though it found not enough data on range and growth. Load gained by shortening your range is not progress.

text: "Partial repetitions are always wrong" goes too far, though.
Evidence: moderate for long over short; insufficient for partials over full range

In a review of 8 studies, training at longer muscle lengths, the stretched part of a movement, gave more growth than training at shorter lengths (effect size 0.283, 0.04 to 0.52). The advantage was clear at the far and central parts of the muscle.
The review compared these two partial ranges with each other. It does not show that partials beat a full range.
In practice:
Train through a full range by default.
A partial done on purpose in the stretched position is a fair tool, such as when a joint limits the other part of the range.
A partial done because the load is too heavy is still a mistake. Decide before the set, not after.
A quarter squat cuts out the stretched part, which is the part this evidence favours.
Volume, effort and frequency
The evidence in Building a push session applies. No fixed recovery time for legs, such as 72 hours, is established.

In practice, heavy squats and hinges are demanding, and many people handle them less often than pressing or pulling. Test that against your own log. The claim that calves recover fast enough to train daily is not established. Train them as often as you can sustain and progress.
How to progress
The three models from the push chapter apply. Adjusting by feel can suit squats and hinges, since it may catch a tired day before your technique breaks down.

For strength, the ACSM links loads of 80% of your one-repetition maximum or more with greater gains. For growth, load from 30% to 100% made no difference, which is how a leg extension can build quadriceps despite a modest number on the stack.

text: Warm-up

Use the same three parts, aimed at your hips and ankles. Warm-up sets matter most here, where your main lift is heaviest. Tight ankles can limit squat depth. It is not established that warming them up changes your results, so test whether your own depth improves, and keep the work if it does.
Across the week
A leg session's demand often makes it the session to plan around. Remember that a heavy hinge shares work with pulling sessions through your lower back and grip.
Worked example
This is one example, not a prescription.
Slot | Exercise | Sets | Repetitions | Rest
Slot: Main squat; Exercise: Barbell back squat; Sets: 4; Repetitions: 6 to 8; Rest: 2 to 3 min
Slot: Hip hinge; Exercise: Romanian deadlift; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 8 to 10; Rest: 2 to 3 min
Slot: Second quad lift; Exercise: Leg press; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 10 to 12; Rest: 90 sec
Slot: Hamstring isolation; Exercise: Seated leg curl; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 10 to 12; Rest: 75 to 90 sec
Slot: Quad isolation; Exercise: Leg extension; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 12 to 15; Rest: 60 to 90 sec
Slot: Calves; Exercise: Standing calf raise; Sets: 4; Repetitions: 12 to 15; Rest: 60 to 90 sec
Leg press and leg extension are both here on purpose, because they favoured different parts of the quadriceps. The seated curl keeps your hip bent, which holds your hamstrings at a longer length.
Common mistakes
Cutting depth to add load. A quarter squat is a different, easier exercise.
Skipping the hinge. This is a common gap in leg sessions.
Assuming big lifts make isolation useless. Early evidence points the other way.
Bouncing out of the bottom of a squat. Stay in control where the load on your muscles is greatest.
Scheduling by a fixed clock. Use your log.
Skipping calves because progress is slow. Slow is not the same as absent.
Key takeaways
Cover both squat and hip-hinge patterns.
Big lifts and isolation work may develop different parts of a muscle.
Put your main lift first.
Full range is the default. A deliberate partial in the stretched position is defensible. One caused by too much load is not.
No fixed recovery time is established for legs. Check your own log.
Load drives strength. For size, hard sets matter more than the number on the bar.
Chapter overview

Variation is a tool for specific problems, not something your plan needs on a schedule. This chapter covers when changing an exercise is worth it, what it costs, and what a second good selection looks like.
What the evidence says
Evidence: moderate

The ACSM found periodised programmes were not significantly better than non-periodised ones for healthy adults, given good progressive overload, and concluded periodisation is less important than once thought. It found not enough data to say whether varied exercise selection affects growth, and concluded that many forms of resistance training work.

text: So if variation is not needed, changing an exercise should have a real reason. "It has been a while" is not one.

Two other popular reasons are also weak. It is not established that repeating a movement harms your joints when technique and recovery are sound, or that variation protects them. Feeling fresher is a real reason, as a preference. A plan you will follow beats a slightly better one you abandon.
What changing costs

Progress needs a stable reference. An exercise changed every few weeks cannot show improvement, because there is no unbroken run of numbers. A new movement also takes practice, so at first your coordination may limit you before your muscle does.
If you are still progressing on an exercise, keep it.
Good reasons to change
Reason | Grade | What to do
Reason: Joint irritation on one movement; Grade: Practical, and decisive; What to do: Swap to a movement in the same slot that does not cause the symptom. See a clinician if pain continues.
Reason: Equipment not available; Grade: Practical; What to do: Apply the swap test and move on.
Reason: Coverage; Grade: Emerging; What to do: A different exercise may develop a different part of the muscle.
Reason: True stall on one exercise; Grade: Practical; What to do: First rule out the causes in Progressive overload.
Reason: Motivation; Grade: Practical; What to do: Fair. Change something, note it, and accept that your numbers reset.
Reason: "Muscle confusion"; Grade: Insufficient; What to do: Not a demonstrated mechanism, and not a reason.
What stays the same
The slots from Building a push session do not change. Only the exercise in each slot does, chosen with the same four tests. Volume, effort, frequency, progression and warm-up all stay.
Applying the swap test

Main press: flat barbell bench instead of incline dumbbell press. Same pattern and joint action. The barbell takes away the balance demand of two separate weights and lets you lift more. It is a different trade, not a better exercise.
Second press: incline machine press instead of flat machine press. Same pattern and slot, at a different angle.
Isolation slots: pec deck, machine lateral raise, single-arm cable lateral raise, EZ-bar extension and single-arm pushdown each match their counterparts in target and joint action.

An overhead triceps extension loads part of your triceps at a longer length than a pushdown does. Evidence for long lengths comes from comparing partial ranges, mostly in legs, so treat this as a reason to include one, not as proof.

Changing push exercises sets out the position: variation is not required. This chapter gives a second good way to fill the pull slots, and says when that is worth the cost.

Grip and forearms. If your hands limit the set before your back does, move to machine-supported pulling or use straps.
Coverage. Different lines of pull work your back differently, and different exercises may develop different parts of a muscle. The direct evidence is from legs, so this is reasoning.

Main pull: wide-grip lat pulldown instead of a pull-up. Same vertical pattern and joint action, less stability demand and much finer loading steps.
Second pull: seated cable row instead of chest-supported row. Same horizontal pattern. Your free torso adds light trunk work, but also makes it easier to swing.

text: Chapter overview

You do not need to weigh every meal to eat well. A plate split into the right parts gets most meals close: half vegetables and fruit, a quarter grains, a quarter protein, a little healthy fat, and water to drink. The idea comes from Harvard's Healthy Eating Plate; the amounts below come from ICMR-NIN's guidelines for Indian diets.
The plate
One meal on the plate
Vegetables (more than fruit; potatoes do not count) · 0.4 · sabzi, salad, dal-vegetable mixes, greens
Fruit · 0.1 · whole fruit rather than juice
Grains, mostly whole · 0.25 · roti, brown or hand-pounded rice, millets, oats
Protein · 0.25 · dal, paneer, curd, eggs, chicken, fish, soya, chana
Add a small amount of healthy oil for cooking (groundnut, mustard, sesame, rice bran), and drink water, buttermilk, or tea and coffee with little or no sugar.
A day on ICMR's plate
A day's food for about 2,000 kcal
Vegetables, including leafy greens · 400 · half the plate across the day [g or ml a day]
Cereals and millets (raw weight) · 250 · rice, wheat, millets [g or ml a day]
Milk and curd · 300 · ml [g or ml a day]
Fruit · 100 · one medium fruit [g or ml a day]
Pulses, eggs, meat or fish · 85 · raw weight; more for higher protein targets [g or ml a day]
Nuts and seeds · 35 · a small handful [g or ml a day]
Fats and oils · 27 · about 5 to 6 teaspoons, all cooking included [g or ml a day]

These are ICMR-NIN's amounts for a moderately active adult. Your Levlofit plan sets your own calories and protein, so your portions may be bigger or smaller; the shares stay similar. People who train hard usually need more protein than this day gives, which is why your plan adds protein foods. See Protein.

text: How much
Evidence: position stand
The International Society of Sports Nutrition states that 1.4 to 2.0 g of protein per kg of body weight per day is sufficient for most exercising people for building and keeping muscle.
supporting_passage: Based on the current available literature, the position of the Society is as follows:An acute exercise stimulus, particularly resistance exercise, and protein ingestion both stimulate muscle protein synthesis (MPS) and are synergistic when protein consumption occurs before or after resistance exercise.For building muscle mass and for maintaining muscle mass through a positive muscle protein balance, an overall daily protein intake in the range of 1.4-2.0 g protein/kg body weight/day (g/kg/d) is sufficient for most exercising individuals, a value that falls in line within the Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range published by the Institute of Medicine for protein.Higher protein intakes (2.3-3.1 g/kg/d) may be needed to maximize the retention of lean body mass in resistance-trained subjects during hypocaloric periods.There is novel evidence that suggests higher protein intakes (>3.0 g/kg/d) may have positive effects on body composition in resistance-trained individuals (i.e., promote loss of fat mass).Recommendations regarding the optimal protein intake per serving for athletes to maximize MPS are mixed and are dependent upon age and recent resistance exercise stimuli.

text: So think in hours, not minutes, and remember the meal before training counts as well.
Before training
The goal is to feel fuelled and comfortable. Two patterns work:
A normal meal a few hours before. Protein and carbohydrate, with moderate fat and fibre so you are comfortable when you start.
A lighter snack closer to training. Mostly carbohydrate, with some protein, and low in fat and fibre.
Indian options include curd with fruit, poha or upma, oats with milk, a banana with milk, rice with dal, toast with peanut butter, and roti with paneer.
No exact timing is established. What feels comfortable varies with the person and the meal, so try it and see.
Training early, or without eating

Training without food is a scheduling choice. In practice it suits some people and not others. If eating first makes you uncomfortable, train and eat afterwards. If you feel weak or light-headed, eat something small first. If that continues, or if you have diabetes or another medical condition, ask your doctor.
After training
Have a meal with protein and carbohydrate within the next few hours. That is the whole recommendation.
You do not need a shake before leaving the gym. It is also fine if that is the easiest way to reach your daily protein.
When carbohydrate timing really matters
Fast glycogen refuelling plans are for when you need rapid recovery, such as training twice in one day or competing on back-to-back days.

text: What usually goes wrong
Skipping meals to save calories, then overeating later. This is really a total-food problem.
Training after a long gap without food, then blaming the plan. Food belongs on your stall checklist.
Eating a large, fatty, high-fibre meal right before training. It can be uncomfortable.
Trying new food on a day that matters. Test it on an ordinary day first.
Perfecting your timing while your daily total goes unmeasured. Fix the big things first.
Treating a post-workout shake as a requirement. It is a convenience.
Key takeaways
The effect of training lasts at least a day. Think in hours, not minutes.
Total energy and protein come first. Timing is a refinement.
Spreading protein every 3 to 4 hours is the stated ideal.
Fast carbohydrate plans are for rapid recovery, not ordinary training.
Meal frequency is a practical choice.
Training without eating first is a scheduling choice.
Chapter overview
A small budget changes which foods you use, not what your body needs. Total energy, protein and sticking with it still decide your result.
Practical guidance
Prices and availability vary by city, season and household, so most of this chapter is practical advice rather than research. The protein figures come from food composition tables.
The number to compare
When money is tight, compare cost per gram of protein, not price per kilogram. Protein is usually the expensive part of your food, and carbohydrate is usually cheap.
Work it out once

Divide the pack price by the grams of protein in the pack. Do this for the five or six sources you can actually buy. You only need to do it occasionally, and the cheapest food by weight is often not the cheapest protein.

Dry soya chunks and pulses often work out cheap per gram of protein, dairy often sits in the middle, and paneer, whey and meat are often more expensive. Check your own local prices, since this is a starting guess.

These are for planning. Where a pack has a label, trust the label. Curd is useful too, and it can cost less set at home from milk. Check the label on packaged curd for its protein.
Everything else is usually cheap

Rice, atta, oats, potatoes, bananas, and seasonal fruit and vegetables are usually inexpensive. For fat, peanuts, seeds and ordinary cooking oil do the job. If you have money left over, a wider range of vegetables and enough fruit will make your food more pleasant, and healthier.
A low-cost day
Meal | Example | What it adds
Meal: Breakfast; Example: Oats cooked in milk, with a banana; What it adds: Protein from milk, carbohydrate, little skill needed
Meal: Lunch; Example: Rice, dal, a vegetable, curd; What it adds: A standard meal, often close already. A larger serving of dal is an easy upgrade.
Meal: Snack; Example: Peanuts, curd or an egg; What it adds: Cheap protein when you might otherwise skip it
Meal: Dinner; Example: Soya chunk curry with rice or roti, plus a vegetable; What it adds: A big, low-cost protein serving
Notice this is not a special diet. It is an ordinary Indian day with the protein parts made bigger. That is often the cheapest way to your target, and the easiest to keep up.
If you cannot cook
Hostel, shared kitchen, no time or no skill? These still work:
Milk and curd, with no preparation.
Sattu mixed into water or milk.
Roasted chana, which keeps well and travels easily.
Peanuts.
Boiled eggs, if you can boil water.
Oats soaked overnight in milk with fruit.
Whey, if its cost per gram of protein works for you.
If your meals come from a mess or canteen, add to what is served: extra dal or curd at the meal, and a protein snack in your room. You can tell Levlofit about mess meals in your diet settings.
Saving money without losing your target
Buy dry staples in bulk if you can store them. Rice, dal, soya chunks and oats keep well.
Buy seasonal produce. It is usually cheaper.
Cook once, eat several times. Batch cooking dal or chana saves fuel and time.
Carry water. Sugary drinks cost money and add calories without much fullness.
Make curd or paneer at home if you can.
Compare supplements with food before you buy.
Batch cooking and food safety
Batch cooking is a main budget strategy, but it can be risky if handled carelessly, particularly with cooked rice and pulses in hot weather.
Cool cooked food quickly, refrigerate it promptly and reheat it thoroughly. Do not keep leftovers at room temperature for long. If your fridge is unreliable, cook smaller amounts more often.
Common mistakes
Assuming eating well must be expensive. Soya chunks, dal, eggs and milk can be affordable.
Buying supplements before food. Food often gives you more protein for the money.
Skipping meals to save money. It cuts energy, and can lead to overeating later.
Paying for "fitness" branded food. Compare its protein and price with ordinary food.
Forgetting to count dal. Protein already in your meals counts.
Cutting protein first. It is the part most likely to go when money is short, and one that matters most.
Key takeaways
Your targets do not change with your budget. Your foods do.
Compare cost per gram of protein.
Soya chunks, dal, chana, milk, curd and eggs can carry most of the load.
The cheapest plan is usually an ordinary Indian day with bigger protein servings.
No-cook options work: sattu, curd, roasted chana, peanuts and soaked oats.
Take care with cooked rice and pulses in warm weather.

text: Chapter overview

One common claim says drink constantly and hit a fixed daily target. Another says thirst handles everything. The evidence is more contextual. Past a certain point, losing fluid impairs performance. Thirst is a good guide in some conditions and a poor one in others. And drinking too much can be dangerous.

text: The number that matters
Evidence: moderate

Dehydration of 2% of body mass or more is associated with poorer temperature control, more strain on the heart and, in many conditions, poorer aerobic performance. text: Chapter overview
Restaurants, travel, weddings and festivals are a permanent part of life. A way of eating that only works in your own kitchen will not last.
The ISSN says the long-term success of a diet depends on sticking with it. So how you handle the exceptions matters. The advice below is practical judgement, not research.

text: Timescale is the whole argument
Timescale | What it tells you
Timescale: One meal; What it tells you: Very little, against a week or a month.
Timescale: One day; What it tells you: Little on its own.
Timescale: A week; What it tells you: The shortest span worth reacting to.
Timescale: A month or more; What it tells you: Where your body composition really responds.
One large restaurant meal is only a part of a week's food. The bigger cost often comes from your reaction to it.
The "80/20 rule"

You may hear that 80% of your meals should be nutritious and 20% flexible. The idea is sound: most of your food should serve your goals, and some can be flexible. The exact ratio is a memory aid, not a finding. Build a week that mostly works, and stop auditing the exceptions.
Eating out
You are usually choosing from someone else's options, so aim for the best available choice.
What to do | How
What to do: Find the protein; How: Paneer, dal, chana, curd, eggs, chicken, fish or tofu. Restaurant meals often have plenty of energy and less protein.
What to do: Notice the oil; How: Deep-fried dishes and rich gravies usually have far more calories than tandoori, grilled, roasted or dry versions.
What to do: Count your drinks; How: Sugary drinks, juice and alcohol add calories with little fullness.
What to do: Watch portions; How: Sharing, or stopping when comfortable, often works better than deciding beforehand to eat half.
What to do: Add volume; How: A salad, raita or vegetable side can replace some richer food.
Do not arrive starving
Skipping meals to "save" calories for an event can backfire and lead to eating more. Eat normally through the day, with protein, then enjoy the event.
Alcohol
It contains calories, without much fullness, so they are easy to miss.
Mixers add more, especially soft drinks and juices.
It can disturb your sleep, even if it makes you drowsy.
It can loosen your food decisions during and after drinking.
Levlofit makes no health recommendation about drinking. That is a personal and medical matter. If your progress has stalled and alcohol is regular, count it before you decide your plan has failed.
Travel
Carry protein. Roasted chana, peanuts, whey in a shaker, or milk cartons where available.
Carry water. Travel days make it easy to drink too little.
Do not skip meals because the options are imperfect. An imperfect meal usually beats a missed one.
Expect your weight to move for reasons other than fat. Salt, fluid, fibre and timing all change. Your seven-day average will smooth this out.
Walk. Travel is otherwise very still.
A missed week of training does not undo months of work. The bigger risk is returning at your old loads straight away, so ease back in.
Festivals and celebrations
Indian festival seasons can be long and full of food. Treating each one as a threat is miserable and unnecessary.
Eat normally, with protein, during the day.
Eat what you want at the occasion.
Return to your usual pattern at the next meal, not next Monday.
Do not punish yourself with extra exercise or restriction afterwards.
Compensation is the pattern to watch
Skipping meals before an event, exercising to "cancel" food, restricting hard the next day, or feeling a lot of guilt about a meal can turn an ordinary occasion into a problem.

These can also be early signs of a difficult relationship with food. If the pattern continues, feels hard to control or affects your daily life, talk to a qualified clinician or dietitian. This Handbook does not diagnose or treat eating disorders.
When choices are limited
Hostel mess, conference food, long journeys, family obligations. In order of usefulness:
Take the protein that is available.
Add vegetables or fruit, if there are any.
Drink water, not sweetened drinks.
Eat until comfortable, not full.
Stop thinking about it afterwards.
Common mistakes
Believing one meal matters. Over a month, it matters little.
Skipping meals beforehand. It can make you eat more overall.
Declaring a "cheat day". One flexible meal can grow into a whole day.
Giving up on the week after one meal. This costs far more than the meal.
Punishing yourself with exercise. Training is not a payment for food.
Forgetting drinks. They can add up quickly.
Reacting to the scale after travel. Wait for your average.
Key takeaways
Your body responds over months. One meal is small, and your reaction can cost more.
80/20 is a memory aid, not a finding.
Eating out: find the protein, notice the oil, count your drinks and do not arrive starving.
Alcohol adds calories and can disturb your sleep.
Travelling: carry protein and water, and ignore the scale for a few days.
Watch for compensating. Get support if it becomes a pattern.

text: What sleep loss costs

text: Chapter overview
Stress is usually described as something that slows your recovery. The better-supported effect is simpler: stress makes you less likely to train at all. That changes what you should do about it.
What stress does to training
Evidence: moderate to strong for the effect on behaviour
Of 55 prospective studies, 76.4% found that psychological stress predicted less physical activity or more sitting. Among higher-quality studies, it was 85.7%.

text: The most useful point in this chapter
The habit itself can protect you. The early work of making training automatic may be what keeps you going through stressful periods later.
What this chapter does not claim

It is not established here that stress directly slows your physical recovery between sessions. It is plausible, and stress can disturb your sleep, which does affect performance. None of the advice below depends on that claim.

Exercise may also help how you feel. A large review of trials found walking, jogging, yoga and strength training eased depression, with effects that seemed comparable to some established treatments, though with less confidence in the evidence. That is useful. It does not make training a replacement for care. For stress specifically, the review above found only early evidence that stress management combined with exercise protects activity levels.

Adjusting your training

Let your training move with your life. Cutting sets for a demanding month and restoring them later keeps you consistent. Keeping the same plan and missing sessions does not. Levlofit can make a day lighter or move a session, or offer fewer days if you keep missing them.

If performance is falling across several exercises, add stress to your checklist, alongside sleep and food.
Practical measures
These are ordinary, low-cost habits, not tested training methods.
Protect your sleep first. Think time in bed.
Keep training scheduled, at lower volume. The habit protects you.
Keep meals regular. Protein and total food can slip during hard weeks.
Cut other commitments before training, if you can.
Take breaks during long work or study, get outdoors when possible, and talk to people you trust.
Slow your breathing when you feel overwhelmed.
When to get support
Beyond a training handbook
Talk to a qualified mental health professional, a doctor or someone you trust if you have:
Low mood, anxiety or loss of interest in things you enjoy, lasting for weeks.
Feeling overwhelmed in a way that affects your daily life, relationships, work or study.
Sleep problems that continue despite enough time in bed.
Large changes in appetite or weight that you did not intend.
Using alcohol or other substances to manage how you feel.
Training that feels compulsive: distress at missing a session, training through illness or injury, or exercising to make up for food.
Thoughts of harming yourself. Do not wait. In India, you can call Tele-MANAS on 14416 at any time, or your local emergency services.
Levlofit does not diagnose or treat mental health conditions. Asking for support is not a failure of discipline.

Treating a stressful month as a plan failure. Diagnose before you change anything.
Expecting training to fix a medical problem. It may help. It does not replace care.

Reduce on purpose and keep your schedule, rather than missing weeks.

text: Chapter overview

Recovery tools are sold on a promise: use them and you will adapt faster. Several have evidence for making you less sore, which is a smaller claim. And one popular tool has evidence of harming the strength gains you train for, so it comes first.
Cold-water immersion: be careful
Evidence: moderate, and negative for strength

text: Deciding whether a tool is worth it
Are sleep, food and training volume handled? If not, no tool will make up for them.
What are you buying? Usually feeling better. That is fine, as long as you know it.
What does it cost? Money, time and, for regular cold immersion, possibly strength gains.
In practice
If a tool makes you feel better and you enjoy it, use it. That can help you keep turning up. Just do not spend money expecting results no evidence has promised.
What you do not need
Anything promising faster recovery. No tool here has shown it.
A long routine after every session. You will likely drop it.
A wearable recovery score that overrules your log. Treat it as a weak input.
Supplements sold for recovery. They do not replace sleep or food.
Safety notes
Use these tools sensibly
Cold immersion carries risks from sudden cold and from staying in too long. If you have a heart condition, ask a clinician first. Do not immerse alone in open water.
Saunas and hot baths carry risks with dehydration, alcohol, pregnancy and some medical conditions.
Massage guns and deep pressure should not be used over an injury, joint, bone or the neck, or over an area that is numb, swollen or painful.
Compression is not right for everyone, especially with circulation problems or a history of blood clots.
If you have a diagnosed condition, ask a clinician before trying any of these.
Common mistakes
Routine cold plunges after lifting. See above.
Buying tools before fixing sleep and food.
Reading "less soreness" as "faster recovery". They are different claims.
Ranking every recovery method on one scale. Sleep and a massage gun are not the same kind of thing.
Key takeaways
Sleep, food and sensible training volume come first. The rest is optional.
Several tools reduce soreness, on weak evidence.
Regular cold-water immersion harmed strength gains. Do not make it a routine if you lift for strength.
Foam rolling and massage guns are fine for comfort.
Feeling better is a fair reason to use something. Just call it that.

text: Deliberate habit work helps, by a modest amount. Be sceptical of anyone promising a system that transforms your consistency.
Problem solving is simple: work out what usually stops you, and decide in advance what you will do when it happens.
Missing a day is not a relapse
In one well-known study, missing one opportunity did not materially affect habit formation. One missed session is a missed session. Most of the damage comes from what you decide next.
What happened | Reasonable response
What happened: Missed one session; Reasonable response: Train at your next planned time. Nothing else changes.
What happened: Ate a meal outside your plan; Reasonable response: Make your next meal normal.
What happened: Missed a week for exams, work or illness; Reasonable response: Return at a manageable load. Do not try to make up the sessions.
What happened: Missed a month or more; Reasonable response: Treat it as a restart, not a failure.
"Never miss twice" is a catchy saying, not a finding.
Habits to consider first
This is a menu, not a schedule, since self-selected habits did better. The order is not based on a direct comparison.

text: Common mistakes
Expecting automatic behaviour in three weeks. It often takes about two months or longer.
Following someone else's habit plan. Self-selected habits did better.
Starting several habits at once. You may conclude you lack discipline when none stick.
Treating one missed day as failure.
Expecting habits to replace training, sleep and protein. They support those things.
Judging a training habit by how it feels. Look at your attendance over weeks.
Key takeaways
Median time to form a habit was about 59 to 66 days, with individuals from 4 to 335 days.
Habit programmes work, by a modest amount.
Choose your own habit, attach it to a steady cue, and give it about two months.
Plan for what usually stops you.
One missed session does not undo the process.

text: Chapter overview

The Nutrition volume covered how energy balance works. This chapter is about running a deficit for months: what protects your muscle, how far to trust a body-fat reading, and when getting leaner stops being a physique project and becomes a health problem.

text: You cannot choose where it comes off

Training one body part is a poor way to lose the fat over it. Expect that fat to change as your overall body fat changes. Later chapters in this volume are about building what is underneath, which is a separate job.
Body-fat percentage is a weaker number than it looks
Evidence: moderate, from one study

Three body-fat scanners using electrical impedance were compared with a DEXA scan in 93 people. Agreement was unacceptable for a consumer scale (0.61), poor for a gym analyser (0.88) and moderate for a medical analyser (0.91).
When 36 people retested after 12 weeks, the subtle changes in body fat did not agree between these devices and DEXA.
All three repeated well within a session. Consistent is not the same as accurate.

So treat a body-fat reading as a wide band, not an exact figure. A scale reading of 17.4% is false precision. Your waist measurement, seven-day average weight, training log and photos are more practical. The body-fat tool in Levlofit gives an estimate too, so read it the same way.

text: Chapter overview
The V-taper is the contrast between your shoulder and upper-back width and your waist. It is a popular goal, often sold with claims that do not hold up.
Wanting one is an aesthetic preference, not a health or performance target. This chapter is about what is achievable, not whether it is worth achieving.
Three contributors, two of them trainable
Contributor | Trainable? | Status
Contributor: Skeleton: shoulder and hip width, rib cage; Trainable?: No, in adults; Status: Bone width does not widen with training once you have finished growing.
Contributor: Muscle over the frame: shoulders, lats, upper back; Trainable?: Yes; Status: Ordinary muscle growth.
Contributor: Body fat, especially at the waist; Trainable?: Yes, but not selectively; Status: You cannot train your waist lean.
So two people with the same plan and effort can end up with different tapers. Much of that difference is likely to be skeletal, and it is no failure of motivation.
Building the muscle
What drives growth in your shoulders and lats is the same as anywhere else: enough weekly work directed at the muscle, progressed over time, with diminishing returns as sets rise.

text: Exercise choice: reasonable, not decisive

The claim that one exercise builds one part of a muscle has thin support. The direct evidence here is one lower-body study. Doing exercises that load a muscle in different positions is sensible and possibly useful. None of these is required.
Target | Usual choices
Target: Shoulders; Usual choices: Overhead presses and lateral raises
Target: Lats; Usual choices: Pull-ups and pulldowns
Target: Upper back; Usual choices: Supported and cable rows
Target: Rear shoulders; Usual choices: Face pulls and reverse flys
Target: Upper chest; Usual choices: Incline presses
The waist: three common claims
Claim | Position
Claim: "Heavy core and oblique work thickens your waist, so avoid it."; Position: Not established. This is a belief, and no reason to skip trunk work.
Claim: "Vacuums and hollowing narrow your waist."; Position: Not established.
Claim: "Train your abs to lose the fat over them."; Position: Do not rely on it. Overall fat loss is what changes this.
What really changes how your waist looks is your overall body fat, which is neither quick nor selective.
Measure your waist, not a ratio
Use a tape at the same spot every few weeks. Shoulder-to-waist targets online, including the "golden ratio", have no validated basis, so this Handbook gives none.
Posture and looking wider
How you stand changes how you look in a photo. That is a claim about appearance, not health. Posture and movement looks at the health claims.
Common mistakes
Expecting training to widen your bones. It adds muscle over them.
Skipping trunk work to protect your waist. That belief is not established.
Building a plan around sculpting regions. The evidence is thin.
Training your abs to reveal them. That comes from overall fat loss.
Adding shoulder and back sets without cutting elsewhere. It costs recovery.
Chasing a published ratio. There is no validated target.
Key takeaways
Bone is fixed, muscle responds to training, and fat cannot be lost selectively.
Shoulders and lats grow on the same dose-response as anything else.
Vary your exercises sensibly, but do not plan around sculpting.
Your waist responds to overall fat loss.
Two people with the same effort will still look different.
Chapter overview
Bringing up a weak muscle is a popular topic with little direct research. This chapter gives you the one lever with evidence, what it costs, and what the rest of the usual advice is worth.
What "lagging" means
Meaning | Status
Meaning: A muscle you have trained less, which is smaller or weaker as a result; Status: Real, and you can address it. Your log can show this.
Meaning: A muscle you would prefer to look different; Status: A preference, often a comparison with a different skeleton.
Only the first responds to more training. Muscle shape and limb length are individual, and exercise choice will not rewrite them.
The one lever with evidence
Evidence: moderate
Muscle growth rises with weekly sets for that muscle, with diminishing returns as sets rise.

text: Extra sets are not free
Recovery has a cost. Adding work without removing any is a recovery decision disguised as a physique decision.

In practice, make it a trade: raise sets for the target muscle and lower them somewhere you are happy to hold steady for a while. Because returns shrink at higher volumes, a well-trained muscle may lose little from giving up a few sets. That is reasoning, not a tested result.

text: Finding a weak point honestly
People who train can see themselves as smaller than they are, and that worry can become a medical problem. These tools are more reliable than your impression:
Method | Good for
Method: Your training log; Good for: Showing a movement you have trained or progressed less. Often the most reliable sign.
Method: Photos in fixed conditions; Good for: Useful over months, not month to month.
Method: Tape measurements; Good for: Cheap and repeatable.
Method: An experienced second opinion; Good for: Reasonable, but still an opinion.
Method: "Which muscle tires first in a big lift"; Good for: Not validated as a sign of a weak muscle.
Left and right are a different question
Small differences between sides are normal. It is not established that single-side work corrects them. Marked or painful differences need a clinician, not a special training block.
How long this takes

Longer than most specialisation plans claim. A muscle that is behind may be months or years of work behind, and returns shrink as you add sets. A block lasting a few weeks may show up in your log and not yet in a photo. Judge it by your log.

text: What not to do
Add sets everywhere at once. Trade instead.
Stop training muscles that are ahead. That is a slower route to balance.
Change your plan every few weeks. Novelty does not solve this.
Treat your anatomy as a training problem. Shape and limb length do not respond to exercise choice.
Copy someone else's specialisation routine without knowing their training history.
Common mistakes
Believing an exercise targets one region. That has thin support.
Treating "train it first" as a growth technique.
Ignoring the recovery cost of extra sets.
Judging a six-week block by photos.
Confusing a real training gap with a preference, or with a preoccupation that needs help.
Key takeaways
More weekly sets for the muscle is the one established lever, with shrinking returns.
Trade sets rather than only adding them.
Exercise order, cues and exercise choice are weak tools for this.
Your anatomy is not a lagging muscle.
Judge the block by your log. The mirror runs on a longer clock.

The familiar story says certain postures are "poor", weak backs and tight chests cause them, and exercises correct them. The evidence does not support that story as stated. Posture is associated with some outcomes, and has not been shown to cause them. Most of the practical advice stays. What changes is why: comfort, strength and appearance, not correction.
Posture and back pain
Evidence: no consensus on cause

A review of 41 systematic reviews looked at spine posture, physical activity and low back pain. They reported both positive and null associations for spine posture, prolonged standing, sitting, bending and twisting, awkward postures and heavy physical work.

Forward head posture and neck pain
Evidence: association in adults, not established as cause
A review of 15 cross-sectional studies found adults with neck pain had more forward head posture than those without. In adolescents there was no significant difference. Age played an important role.

text: All the studies were cross-sectional, which means they measured people at one point in time, so this design cannot show which came first.

The missing link in adolescents is interesting. If this posture simply caused neck pain, you might expect the link at all ages. It might instead reflect age, or people in pain holding themselves differently. That is reasoning, not a finding.
What this means for the advice
Usual framing | What this Handbook says
Usual framing: "Signs of poor posture"; What this Handbook says: Postural variations. They are descriptions, not diagnoses.
Usual framing: "A weak upper back causes rounded shoulders"; What this Handbook says: Not established. This is a mechanical story.
Usual framing: "Tight chest muscles pull your shoulders forward"; What this Handbook says: Not established. Stretching does not lengthen muscle anyway.

Usual framing: "Better alignment means safer lifting"; What this Handbook says: Not established here. Technique is a sensible default.
Usual framing: "Good posture improves your appearance"; What this Handbook says: Fair, as a claim about appearance.
The advice that stays, and why
Practice | Honest reason
Practice: Train your upper back; Honest reason: It is a major muscle group that responds to training.
Practice: Move regularly during long sitting; Honest reason: Reasonable and low-cost, for comfort and activity.
Practice: Use a workstation you find comfortable; Honest reason: Comfort is reason enough.
Practice: Stretch your chest and front shoulders, if you like; Honest reason: It can improve range over months. Loaded full-range training also does this.

Practice: Change position through the day; Honest reason: Since no single correct posture is established here, moving around is a reasonable default.
The short version
There is no one posture you must achieve. Move often, and train your upper back for the same reasons you train everything else.
Pain is a separate question
Get it checked
Nothing in this chapter is advice about pain. If your neck or back pain lasts, see a qualified clinician instead of starting a correction programme.
Get checked promptly if pain spreads into an arm or leg, or comes with numbness, tingling or weakness.
Get checked promptly if pain follows a fall, collision or other injury.
Get checked promptly if pain wakes you at night, or no position relieves it.
Get checked promptly if pain comes with fever, unexplained weight loss or a history of cancer.
Any change in bladder or bowel control, or numbness around the groin or inner thighs, is an emergency.
Common mistakes
Treating a postural variation as an injury waiting to happen. That cause is not established.
Buying a correction programme sold on that claim.
Reading the adult link as proof of cause. The studies cannot show it.
Holding one "correct" position for hours. Move instead.
Stretching to lengthen a muscle. It does not do that.
Using posture work instead of getting pain checked.
Key takeaways
There is no consensus that posture or physical exposure causes low back pain.
Forward head posture is linked with neck pain in adults, not in adolescents, from one-time-point studies only.
Train your upper back for training reasons.
Move often. No single position is established as correct.
Lasting pain needs a clinician.

text: Purpose: Motivating you; Status: Not established. Numbers you feel you must satisfy may not help.
Purpose: Proving your plan works; Status: Too much to ask. It can show whether you are progressing.
Every measurement has error
A reading is the real value plus error. That error comes from three places.
Source | What it looks like | What to do
Source: The tool; What it looks like: It disagrees with reality. Body-fat scanners agreed poorly with DEXA on 12-week change.; What to do: Choose tools with less error.
Source: Your technique; What it looks like: You do it a little differently each time.; What to do: Fix the method: same conditions, same spot, same person.
Source: Your body; What it looks like: Water, food, salt, the menstrual cycle and time of day all move it.; What to do: Average repeated readings, such as a seven-day weight average.
When a number means nothing
React to a change only when it is larger than the error of what measured it. Many weekly changes are not.
Measure | Main problem | Sensible interval
Measure: Body weight; Main problem: Daily swings; Sensible interval: Weekly, using a seven-day average
Measure: Tape measurements; Main problem: Technique; Sensible interval: Monthly, by the same person
Measure: Photos; Main problem: Lighting, pose and pump; Sensible interval: Take monthly, compare every few months
Measure: Logged loads and reps; Main problem: Least error, since these are counts; Sensible interval: Every session

A photo is one of the noisiest tools in this volume, and the method below exists to reduce that noise. Used well, with fixed conditions and long gaps, it shows the thing you care about. Used casually, it shows the lighting.
This chapter is practical guidance. No study here sets the best method or interval.
What changes between photos
What varies | Effect
What varies: Light direction and hardness; Effect: Often the largest. Overhead or side light adds definition, and flat front light removes it.
What varies: Pose, stance and tension; Effect: Changes your outline. Flexed against relaxed is not a fair comparison.
What varies: Camera distance, height and lens; Effect: Changes how your proportions look.
What varies: Time of day, food, fluid, salt and pump; Effect: The same daily changes that move your weight, made visible.
What varies: Tan, hair and clothing; Effect: Changes how defined you look, with no real change.
Why before-and-after marketing works
All of these can be changed on purpose in an afternoon. If a transformation photo changes more than one, it is not evidence of anything.
Fix the conditions
Fix | Error it removes
Fix: Same room, light and time of day; Error it removes: Lighting, and some daily variation
Fix: Camera on a fixed surface at a marked height and distance; Error it removes: Perspective
Fix: Same stance, with feet on the same marks; Error it removes: Pose
Fix: Relaxed, every time; Error it removes: Tension. Relaxed is easier to repeat than flexed.
Fix: Morning, before eating; Error it removes: Food and fluid
Fix: Not straight after training; Error it removes: Pump
Fix: Front, both sides and back, every time; Error it removes: Choosing flattering angles

How often to take them, and how often to look

Action: Take; Interval: Every four weeks; Why: Cheap, and you can never go back and take last year's.
Action: Compare; Interval: Every three to six months; Why: A month's change is often smaller than the photo's error.

text: How often
These intervals are practical guidance. No study here sets the best one.
Interval | Verdict
Interval: Weekly or more; Verdict: Not recommended. Expected change is smaller than the error.
Interval: Every four weeks; Verdict: A sensible default.
Interval: Every three months; Verdict: Better when gaining muscle, since change is slower.
Reading changes honestly
What you see | What it supports
What you see: Waist down several centimetres over months, lifts holding; What it supports: Fits fat loss with muscle kept. This takes months.
What you see: Arm or chest up 1 cm in a month; What it supports: Nothing yet. Wait.
What you see: Everything up together; What it supports: Unclear. Use your weight trend and log.
What you see: Nothing changed in three months; What it supports: Worth looking into, but check your log first.
What you see: One reading far from the trend; What it supports: Probably technique. Measure again.
Do not act on one reading
One tape measurement does not justify a decision that day. If a measurement decides your mood, whether you eat or whether you train, stop measuring and see a clinician.
Common mistakes
Reporting more precision than a tape can give.
Comparing your number with a published standard or another person.
Measuring eight sites and treating the noisiest as a trend.
Taking one reading instead of three.
Changing your tape, spot, time or measurer.
Sucking in, or measuring after eating.
Acting on a 1 cm change.
Key takeaways
Self-measuring can be fairly accurate, but small changes still sit inside the error.
Compare only with your own past measurements, taken the same way.
Measure two sites, take three readings, and record the middle one.
Every four weeks at most, or three months when gaining.
One centimetre is not a finding.
Chapter overview

Body weight is the cheapest measurement in this Handbook, and among the most misread. A decent scale has little error, while your body's daily changes are large. That combination decides everything below.
The rule
Use a seven-day average
Judge your weight by a seven-day average, not one reading. Weigh most days in the same conditions, average the last seven readings, and compare that average week to week.
Averaging works because daily swings partly cancel out. Your body does not change when you take an average. Your measurement improves.
A rolling average also updates every day, so one missed weigh-in does little harm.
What the scale is weighing
Part | How fast it moves
Part: Body fat; How fast it moves: Weeks to months. At 0.5 to 1% of body weight a week, an 80 kg person loses about 0.4 to 0.8 kg a week.
