A worked example
These are example numbers from one week in a fat-loss phase, not a target.
Day | Reading
Day: Monday; Reading: 74.0 kg
Day: Tuesday; Reading: 74.4 kg
Day: Wednesday; Reading: 73.9 kg
Day: Thursday; Reading: 74.2 kg
Day: Friday; Reading: 74.1 kg
Day: Saturday; Reading: 73.8 kg
Day: Sunday; Reading: 74.0 kg

The average is 74.1 kg. Someone looking only at Tuesday thinks they gained. Someone looking only at Saturday thinks they are losing quickly. It is the same week, and only next week's average adds information.

This is where your numbers turn into decisions. Mostly, its job is to stop you. In most months, the right action is to change nothing, and that is the review working. Levlofit's weekly report gives you the raw material.

Evidence: moderate

text: Problem solving means working out what usually stops you, and deciding what you will do when it happens. The rest of this chapter is reasoning from the measurement errors in this volume.
Why most months should end in no change
Reason | What it means
Reason: Your tools are noisy; What it means: Much month-to-month movement is measurement, not you.
Reason: Reviewing many numbers guarantees a bad one; What it means: With six noisy numbers, at least one is likely to look alarming by chance.
Choose your decision number before you look

Decide in advance which one number decides things, such as your seven-day weight average when losing fat or your log when gaining. Treat the others as context, so you cannot go looking for the number that justifies what you already wanted to do.
Decision rules
What your number shows | Action
What your number shows: Moving as intended; Action: Change nothing.
What your number shows: Weight average flat for two or more weeks, goal is fat loss; Action: Eat a little less or move a little more. Change one thing.
What your number shows: Weight falling too fast; Action: Slow down. Slower loss can better protect lean mass in leaner people.
supporting_passage: Slower rates of weight loss can better preserve lean mass (LM) in leaner subjects. 4) Diets focused primarily on accruing LM are driven by a sustained caloric surplus to facilitate anabolic processes and support increasing resistance-training demands.

text: What your number shows: Two or three sessions of a lift flat or falling; Action: Check sleep, food, stress and volume before changing your plan.
What your number shows: Several lifts flat for weeks, with those in order; Action: See Breaking through plateaus and Deload week.
What your number shows: Tape or photos disagree with a rising log; Action: Trust your log.
What your number shows: Lasting pain or red-flag symptoms; Action: Not a training decision. See a clinician.
What your number shows: Signs of low energy availability or body image distress; Action: Stop this phase and see a clinician. No physique target overrides this.
Change one thing
If you change your training and your food in the same month, your next review cannot tell you which one mattered.
What to review, in order
Order | What to ask
Order: 1. Attendance; What to ask: Did your plan actually happen? A month of missed sessions does not test your plan.
Order: 2. Your training log; What to ask: Loads and reps per lift, across the month.
Order: 3. Your decision number; What to ask: The one you chose in advance.
Order: 4. Inputs; What to ask: Sleep, stress and food, to explain what you saw.
Order: 5. Photos, every few months; What to ask: Skip the months when a comparison would only be noise.
Order: 6. One obstacle, and a plan for it; What to ask: The problem-solving step.
Avoid rating things like "satisfaction" out of five and tracking them as if they were measurements. Attendance can be counted. Satisfaction cannot.
Motivation
Noticing that you got better at something supports your sense of competence, which is linked with continuing to exercise. Keep that. Do not treat this review as a test you pass or fail.

text: Chapter overview
Many people stop training. What distinguishes those who do not? The evidence has a partial answer, and it does not come down to willpower.
Your reasons
Evidence: moderate

A review of 66 studies found consistent support for a link between more autonomous motivation and exercise. Valuing the outcome tended to predict starting, while intrinsic motivation better predicted long-term exercise. Feeling competent also predicted exercise. Most studies were non-experimental, so this shows association, not proven cause.

[...] The literature is also consistent in that competence satisfaction and more intrinsic motives positively predict exercise participation across a range of samples and settings. [...] The majority of studies have employed descriptive (i.e., non-experimental) designs but similar results are found across cross-sectional, prospective, and experimental designs.

Your reduced week
When a month is hard, choose between your full plan and a smaller one, not your full plan and nothing. These are practical suggestions.
What gets in the way | Reduced version
What gets in the way: No time; Reduced version: Do fewer exercises. Cut volume on purpose instead of watering down every set.
What gets in the way: Travelling; Reduced version: Do whatever is available.
What gets in the way: Illness; Reduced version: Rest, and return at a lower load.
What gets in the way: High stress; Reduced version: Protect attendance over intensity. The documented cost of stress is missed sessions.

Moving up in any discipline should mean showing a real ability, not just finishing a number of weeks. These six simple field tests give you an honest starting point. They need little more than a bar and a stopwatch, and all are optional.

What a field test can tell you
Evidence: moderate, with an important limit

One study of field tests including pull-ups and push-ups found they were not valid measures of absolute strength, but were valid for strength relative to body weight. The study was in 94 children aged 9 to 10, so it applies to adults only by reasoning.

text: In practice, a push-up or pull-up count is a repeatable way to compare yourself with yourself over months. Do not treat it as a stand-in for a one-repetition maximum.
The six tests
Warm up first, and stop when your form breaks. These are practical test descriptions.
Strict push-ups. Full range, chest near the floor, no sagging hips, until form breaks.
Strict pull-ups or chin-ups. Start from a dead hang, chin clears the bar, no swinging.
Dead hang. Time how long your grip holds.
Plank or hollow-body hold. Time until the position collapses.
1 km run. Flat ground, at your own pace, timed.
Standing broad jump. Take off and land on two feet. Measure to your heels. Take your best of three.
These are maximal efforts

If you have a joint, tendon or heart condition that a hard test could aggravate, skip that test and ask your doctor first. Stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness. A partial baseline is still useful.

Retest every 8 to 12 weeks if you want a check, at the start of a new block rather than at the end of a tiring one. This interval is practical guidance. A result that has not moved is information, not failure. Change one thing at a time.

These tests measure how well you move your own body.
They are good for comparing yourself over time, and poor stand-ins for maximum strength.
The main study behind this was in children, so treat its findings as a guide.
All of them are optional. Skip any your health makes unwise.

text: Chapter overview

Much fitness content assumes a full gym and treats everything else as a compromise. Levlofit asks what you actually have, and builds your plan around that. This chapter explains the thinking, so you can make good swaps yourself.
What drives results

The ACSM concludes that many forms of resistance training work, and calls for programmes to be fitted to the person. A well-run bodyweight plan and a well-run barbell plan are both real training. A poor substitution, made without knowing it, is the real problem.

Fixtures matter too

Some movements need somewhere to hang or stand. A pull-up needs a bar, and a box jump needs a box. A doorway pull-up bar is one of the cheapest items that can open up a lot of pulling work. Fit it securely, follow its limits and test it before you trust your weight to it.
When nothing fits

If a movement needs equipment you lack, use the swap test from Building a push session: same movement pattern, same joint action. If nothing matches, choose the closest option and be honest with yourself that it is a different exercise. You can tell Levlofit what you have, and ask it to swap an exercise.
Limits of bodyweight training
Adding load is harder, so use reps, slower progressions and harder positions.
Using only body mass did not significantly improve range of motion in one review, so you may want separate mobility work.

text: Chapter overview

This closing chapter walks through how to put training into a week, then answers some common questions. It is practical guidance built on the rest of this Handbook. Your Levlofit plan does this for you, and this chapter helps you understand and adjust it.
Building a week, in order
Start with your main goal. It has first claim on your days.
Add other goals at a smaller, steady dose. See Combining different kinds of training.
Fit it to your equipment. Use what you actually have.
Respect your limits. Remove anything that aggravates a known problem. If your session is short, trim small exercises first.
Set your starting point honestly. Start from where you actually are.
For health, aim for WHO's guidelines as well: 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, or a mix, along with muscle strengthening.

text: The long view

No one calendar suits everyone. A useful pattern is to build the basics before specialising, check your progress at the end of each block, and reduce your training when fatigue says so. A year of training is that cycle repeated. Your goals and equipment can change between cycles.
Troubleshooting
Question | Answer
Question: My extra goal has no room this week.; Answer: You may not have enough days for both. Keep your main goal, trim the extra one, or add a day if you can recover from it.
Question: My skill is stuck on one step.; Answer: Skills move up when you can do the next step with control, not because time has passed. Practise, and retest.

Question: My plan has a different exercise from what I expected.; Answer: You may not have the equipment, or a limit you told Levlofit about may rule it out. Check your equipment and limits, or ask for a swap.
Question: Can I add sparring or partner drills?; Answer: Do this only with a qualified coach in person. See Boxing: solo training.
Question: I keep missing sessions.; Answer: Choose fewer days you can actually keep. Stress and busy periods often show up as missed sessions.
